blocks.text: 1. Access Control

blocks.alt: A user goes through a permission check to allowed content only

blocks.text: Security established that permission checks belong at the retrieval level, before a chunk ever reaches the model. Access Control is the concrete mechanism that enforces exactly who can retrieve which content.
It attaches permission metadata to each chunk and checks it against the requesting user before returning any result.
2. Access Control As A Concrete Implementation
Security named the general principle that a user should only see permitted content.
Access control is the specific mechanism that actually enforces that principle at query time.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Concept","Scope"],"rows":[["Security","General principle of protecting data and access"],["Access control","The specific mechanism enforcing who sees what"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Permission Metadata Attached To Each Chunk
Each chunk carries its own permission tags alongside its embedding, the same metadata filtering covered in Vector Databases.
Without that tag, there is nothing for an access check to actually filter against.
4. Role Based Versus Attribute Based Access Control

blocks.alt: Role-based access control is compared against attribute-based access control

blocks.text: Role based control checks a user's fixed role, while attribute based control checks finer grained properties like department or project, similar in spirit to tagging the entity type in Entity Extraction.
The right granularity depends on how varied the actual permission requirements are.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Model","What it checks"],"rows":[["Role based","A user's fixed role, such as admin or public"],["Attribute based","Finer grained properties like department or project"]]}

blocks.text: 5. Filtering Before Ranking, Not After

blocks.alt: Filtering first is compared against filtering after ranking

blocks.text: Permission filtering must happen before ranking, or a permitted chunk could be pushed out by ones the user was never allowed to see anyway, the same ordering concern behind precision at K versus context precision in Context Precision.
Filtering order matters just as much as the filtering rule itself.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Ranking the top five chunks first and then filtering by permission can leave a user with fewer than five results even when permitted chunks existed further down the unranked list, exactly why filtering must come first.

blocks.text: 6. Access Control Applies To Cached Results Too

blocks.alt: A cached result still needs a permission check

blocks.text: A cached response built for one user's permissions must never be served to a user with different permissions, the same concern behind why not all responses are safe to cache in Response Cache.
Access control checks apply to cache lookups, not just live retrieval.
7. Deny By Default Is The Safer Starting Point

blocks.alt: Deny by default is compared against allow by default, which is riskier

blocks.text: A chunk with no explicit permission tag should be treated as inaccessible, not as freely visible, in keeping with security adding friction by design.
Deny by default fails safely, unlike allow by default, which fails open.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A newly ingested chunk missing its permission tag due to an ingestion bug should remain hidden under deny by default, rather than becoming accidentally visible to everyone under an allow by default policy.

blocks.text: 8. Permission Changes Need To Propagate
A user's revoked permission must actually take effect, not just exist as an unused record, the same staleness problem covered in Caching.
Stale permission data is just as dangerous as stale factual data.
9. Recognizing When Fine Grained Access Control Is Worth Its Complexity

blocks.alt: Different users seeing different data points toward fine-grained access control

blocks.text: A system with varied, overlapping permission needs benefits from fine grained access control.
A system with one simple, uniform permission level needs only a basic access check instead.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Filtering by permission after ranking instead of before, losing permitted chunks to unpermitted ones.
Treating an untagged chunk as accessible by default instead of denying it by default.
Serving a cached response to a user whose permissions differ from the one it was built for.
Failing to propagate a revoked permission, leaving stale access rights in effect.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Access control is the concrete mechanism enforcing exactly who can retrieve which content.
It makes security's general principle of permitted access enforceable at actual query time.
Each chunk needs its own permission metadata for an access check to filter against.
Role based control checks a fixed role; attribute based control checks finer grained properties.
Permission filtering must happen before ranking, or permitted chunks can be crowded out.
Access control checks apply to cache lookups too, not just live retrieval.
A chunk with no permission tag should be denied by default, failing safely rather than open.
A revoked permission must actually propagate and take effect, not remain a stale, unused record.
